name: Anyemaji Godswill
feedback: D1 is strong. You catalogued eight of the ten planted findings with the correct OWASP class, a correct CWE, and a quoted evidence line for each: SQL injection (lines 61-64), unsalted MD5 (line 63), JWT alg:none (lines 41-43), no token expiry (lines 72-77), insecure cookie flag (line 82), hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (line 27), XXE (file:///etc/passwd in 04-import-xxe.xml), and path traversal (the 02:24:02 capture). Your decoy work is exactly right and earns full credit: you named the lines 44-47 HS256 branch, proved it safe at the mechanism level because hash_equals is constant-time and defeats timing attacks, and correctly kept alg:none as a real finding rather than calling it the decoy. What held D1 back is two missing findings, the stored XSS in comments (the 02:18:47 cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443) and the open redirect on the next parameter (02:21:13), so the catalogue is eight of ten, not complete. D2 reconstructs the chain with genuinely verbatim PoCs, including the full forged alg:none token, and reconciles the live hops to real capture lines at 02:15:31 and 02:24:02, with a quantified impact of 312 customers and roughly 63 million naira built on a stated average-balance assumption, which is the right way to do it. The chain is weaker than D1 because you compressed it to five hops and skipped the stored XSS (02:18:47) and open redirect (02:21:13) hops, and the SQLi CVSS is over-scored: you used S:C and A:H for a 10.0, but the login bypass does not touch availability, so the correct vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your alg:none vector matched the key exactly and was justified, which is good. D3 is the standout. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model captures the shared-secret link to the BoltCash microservice, the decoy is restated correctly, the earliest-break argument is sound, and crucially you ordered remediation by effort to risk with real effort estimates (5 minutes, 10 minutes, 2 hours, 2 days) rather than by raw severity, which is exactly what the brief asked for. Your two detection stopgaps are concrete with named fields and false-positive rates, the cookie-pattern SQL query and the XXE WAF regex. D3 lost a little for carrying the same eight-not-ten findings gap and repeating the inflated SQLi 10.0 vector. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites Canon II and Canon I load-bearing, and ties the 72-hour NDPC duty and data-subject notification to the 312 customers, but you named the NDPA breach duty without the section numbers, which are section 40 for notifying the NDPC within 72 hours and section 41 for notifying affected data subjects on high risk. The single most important fix is to stop over-scoring CVSS: drop A:H and reconsider S:U on the SQLi bypass so it reads about 9.1, and make sure every planted finding, including the stored XSS and open redirect you missed, gets its own quoted line.
